title: How I Use Worked Examples
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane describes the worked-example routine he built after reading Michael Pershan's book on the subject, adapting it for his own classroom through trial and error. His key insight is that worked example is often misunderstood as a teacher demonstrating a procedure live on the board, when its actual purpose is the opposite: simplifying the learning moment so students face minimal extraneous demands on attention and working memory while they study a complete, already-solved problem. His routine has four fixed steps: students first read and try to understand a bare-bones solution with nothing to copy, then work through three analysis prompts (often via turn-and-talk), then attempt a closely related problem independently, and finally move to a back-of-handout practice set calibrated to how the analysis stage went. Kane identifies three distinct purposes a worked example can serve - helping students understand a complicated multi-step procedure, helping them apply a general principle across varied situations (illustrated with a floats and anchors example for adding positive and negative numbers), and helping them choose the correct strategy in the first place, illustrated by students who can solve circumference or area problems in isolation but can't tell which is which in a mixed word-problem set. Throughout, he frames the format's value as forcing focus onto the mathematical reasoning behind each step rather than the sequence of procedural moves, which he argues generalizes far better to novel problems.
points: Kane's routine breaks worked-example study into four discrete steps - study the solution, analyse it via three fixed prompts, attempt a similar problem, then practice - deliberately minimizing what's on the page at each stage to reduce cognitive load.

He identifies three distinct instructional purposes worked examples can serve - understanding a complicated procedure, applying a general principle, and choosing between strategies - and matches specific examples to each.

His floats and anchors example for adding positive and negative numbers shows the technique used for principle transfer rather than procedure, asking students to apply an abstract framework across varied problems rather than memorize steps.

The circumference-versus-area confusion example illustrates his choosing a strategy purpose: worked examples aimed not at solving a problem correctly but at correctly identifying which type of problem is in front of the student in the first place.
quotes: A worked example is a complete solution to a problem. The goal is to have students study a worked example as a way to learn some math.

Trying to learn math by solving a problem or being guided through a problem can be overwhelming. The phrase 'worked example' might evoke images of a teacher demonstrating a procedure on the board, but that's not what it means.
The goal of a worked example isn’t just to show students an example, it’s to simplify the learning experience so there are fewer demands on the student’s attention and working memory.
I ask students to read the problem and the solution and try to understand what’s happening. Sometimes I’ll add a few quick pieces of clarification as well.
There’s nothing to copy down and not much else happening on the page. I keep the solution as simple as possible.

That type of knowledge doesn’t generalize very well when students see different types of problems. A worked example creates opportunities to think about why the steps are what they are, setting students up to apply their knowledge in different contexts

I teach circles. Students get good at solving circumference problems as long as I say 'find the circumference,' and solving area problems as long as I say 'find the area.' Then when I give them a mix of word problems they have no idea which is which.
